## 2. Preliminaries

### 2.1.

A convex body in ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ is a convex compact subset of ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ . The support function of a convex body $K$ is defined by $h_{K}(u):=\max_{x\in K}\langle x,u\rangle$ . The Minkowski sum of $K$ with $L$ is defined as $K+L:=\{a+b:a\in K,b\in L\}$ . The Minkowski difference of $K$ and $L$ is defined as $K\div L:=\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}:x+L\subseteq K\}$ . The Minkowski sum can be expressed via support functions as

$$ K+L=\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}:\forall u\in S^{n-1},\,\langle x,u\rangle\leqslant h_{K}(u)+h_{L}(u)\}. $$

This motivates the definition of $K^{t}L^{1-t}$ . Indeed, as above we can write the weighted arithmetic mean $tK+(1-t)L$ as

$$ tK+(1-t)L=\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}:\forall u\in S^{n-1},\,\langle x,u\rangle\leqslant th_{K}(u)+(1-t)h_{L}(u)\}. $$

Hence similarly, for $K$ and $L$ containing the origin in their interior (i.e. $h_{K}(u),h_{L}(u)>0$ for all $u\neq 0$ ), it is natural to define the weighted geometric mean of $K$ and $L$ as

$$ K^{t}L^{1-t}:=\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}:\forall u\in S^{n-1},\,\langle x,u\rangle\leqslant h_{K}(u)^{t}h_{L}(u)^{1-t}\}. $$

Denote by $\mathcal{K}^{n}_{s}$ the set of all origin symmetric convex bodies with nonempty interior. We will only consider the log-BM, log-Minkowski, LLBM for convex bodies in the class $\mathcal{K}^{n}_{s}$ .

### 2.2.

Let us collect some facts about mixed volume that will be used in this note, all of which can be found in [11, Chap.5]. First, the mixed volume can be computed via integrating the support function against the mixed area measure

$$ V(C_{1},...,C_{n})=\frac{1}{n}\int_{S^{n-1}}h_{C_{n}}dS_{C_{1},...,C_{n-1}}. $$

In the case where $C_{1}=\cdots=C_{n-1}=C$ , $S_{C,...,C}$ is equal to $S_{C}$ , the area measure of $C$ . In view of (2), we naturally define the mixed volume of $f\in C(S^{n-1};{\mathbb{R}})$ and convex bodies $C_{1},...,C_{n-1}$ ,

$$ V(f,C_{1},...,C_{n-1}):=\frac{1}{n}\int_{S^{n-1}}fdS_{C_{1},...,C_{n-1}}. $$

Under a linear transformation, the mixed volume behaves in the same way as the usual volume: for $A\in\operatorname{GL}(n,{\mathbb{R}})$ and convex bodies $C_{1},...,C_{n}$ ,

$$ V(A(C_{1}),...,A(C_{n}))=|\det(A)|V(C_{1},...,C_{n}). $$

Let $I$ be an interval segment. Denote by $I^{\perp}$ the orthogonal complement of the direction of $I$ and let $P_{I^{\perp}}$ be the orthogonal projection onto $I^{\perp}$ . Then $h_{P_{I^{\perp}}C}(u)=h_{C}(P_{I^{\perp}}u)$ for all $u\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ . In particular, $h_{P_{I^{\perp}}C}=h_{C}|_{I^{\perp}}$ . The projection formula [11, Theorem 5.3.1] asserts that

$$ V(I,C_{1},...,C_{n-1})=\frac{|I|}{n}V(P_{I^{\perp}}C_{1},...,P_{I^{\perp}}C_{n-1}) $$

where $|I|$ is the length of $I$ . For $f\in C(S^{n-1};{\mathbb{R}})$ , the projection formula extends to

$$ V(I,f,C_{1},...,C_{n-2})=\frac{|I|}{n}V(f|_{I^{\perp}\cap S^{n-1}},P_{I^{\perp}}C_{1},...,P_{I^{\perp}}C_{n-2}), $$

### 2.3.

Mixed volumes and mixed area measures can be extended from convex bodies to a certain class of functions by multilinearity [11, Sec. 5.2]. We denote by $D(S^{n-1})$ the linear space spanned by restrictions of support functions to $S^{n-1}$ . And denote by $D_{s}(S^{n-1})=\{f\in D(S^{n-1})\mid\forall x\in S^{n-1},\,f(x)=f(-x)\}$ the subspace in $D(S^{n-1})$ of origin-symmetric functions. Any $f\in D_{s}(S^{n-1})$ can be written as $f=(h_{K}-h_{L})|_{S^{n-1}}$ with $K,L\in\mathcal{K}^{n}_{s}$ . For such $f$ ,

$$ \displaystyle V(f,C_{1},...,C_{n-1})= \displaystyle V(K,C_{1},...,C_{n-1})-V(L,C_{1},...,C_{n-1}), \displaystyle S_{f,C_{1},...,C_{n-2}}= \displaystyle S_{K,C_{1},...,C_{n-1}}-S_{L,C_{1},...,C_{n-1}}. $$

Note that the first formula is compatible with (3). We also have

$$ V(f,f,C_{1},...,C_{n-2})=V(K,f,C_{1},...,C_{n-2})-V(L,f,C_{1},...,C_{n-2}). $$

## 3. LLBM for Zonoids

In this section we use (1) to give a completely self-contained proof of LLBM for zonoids. The proof will proceed by a double induction. We induct on the dimension, and then for a fixed dimension we induct on the number of interval summands. The latter induction step is done in Lemma 3.1 using the formula (1). Lemma 3.1 also immediately implies Theorem 1.2. The former induction step is done in Proposition 3.4.

### 3.1. Induction on number of interval summands

#### Lemma 3.1.

Let $K\in\mathcal{K}^{n}_{s}$ ( $n\geqslant 2$ ) and let $I$ be a segment centered at the origin such that $K=(K\div I)+I$ and $K\div I\in\mathcal{K}^{n}_{s}$ . Assume $\Delta(P_{I^{\perp}}K,g)\geqslant 0$ for all $g\in D_{s}(S^{n-2})$ . Then for all $f\in D_{s}(S^{n-1})$ , we have

$$ \Delta(K,f)=\Delta(K,\bar{f})\geqslant\Delta(K\div I,\bar{f}). $$

where $\bar{f}=f-ch_{K}$ and $c=n\frac{V(K[n-1],f)}{V(K)}-(n-1)\frac{V(K[n-2],I,f)}{V(K[n-1],I)}$ .

#### Proof.

By Lemma 1.1, $\Delta(K,\bar{f})=\Delta(K,f)$ holds. Denote $K_{t}=(K\div I)+tI$ for $t\in[0,1]$ . We have $K=K_{t}+(1-t)I$ . By the choice of $c$ ,

$$ \frac{V(K[n-1],\bar{f})}{V(K)}=\frac{n-1}{n}\frac{V(K[n-2],I,\bar{f})}{V(K[n-1],I)}. $$

Hence, for any $t\in[0,1]$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{V(K_{t}[n-1],\bar{f})}{V(K_{t})} \displaystyle=\frac{V(K[n-1],\bar{f})-(n-1)(1-t)V(K[n-2],I,\bar{f})}{V(K)-n(1-t)V(K[n-1],I)} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{n-1}{n}\frac{V(K[n-2],I,\bar{f})}{V(K[n-1],I)}=\frac{n-1}{n}\frac{V(K_{t}[n-2],I,\bar{f})}{V(K_{t}[n-1],I)}, $$

where for the first equality we used $K=K_{t}+(1-t)I$ and $V(I,I,\cdot,...,\cdot)=0$ , for the second equality we used (6), for the third equality we used $V(I,I,\cdot,...,\cdot)=0$ again. Note that $\frac{d}{dt}h_{K_{t}}=h_{I}$ , (1) yields

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d}{dt} \displaystyle\Delta(K_{t},\bar{f})=\frac{(n-1)^{2}}{n^{2}}|I|D(P_{I^{\perp}}K_{t},f|_{I^{\perp}})+\frac{1}{n}V(K_{t}[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K_{t}}^{2}}h_{I}), $$

where we used (7). Since $\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K_{t}}^{2}}h_{I}\geqslant 0$ , we have $V(K_{t}[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K_{t}}^{2}}h_{I})\geqslant 0$ . By assumption we have $D(P_{I^{\perp}}K_{t},f|_{I^{\perp}})=D(P_{I^{\perp}}K,f|_{I^{\perp}})\geqslant 0$ . Hence $\frac{d}{dt}\Delta(K_{t},\bar{f})\geqslant 0$ . Therefore $\Delta(K,f)=\Delta(K,\bar{f})\geqslant\Delta(K\div I,\bar{f})$ .

∎

#### Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Let us prove the claim by induction on the dimension $n$ . Since LLBM is true in dimension 1, our claim is a fortiori true in dimension 1. Now assume the claim holds in dimension $n-1\geqslant 1$ and let us prove the claim in dimension $n$ .

Consider $\Delta(K+I_{1}+\cdots+I_{\ell},f)$ , where $I_{1},...,I_{\ell}$ are origin-symmetric segments and $f\in D_{s}(S^{n-1})$ . For any subspace $E$ of $I_{\ell}^{\perp}$ , $\Delta(P_{E}(P_{I_{\ell}^{\perp}}K),h_{C})=\Delta(P_{E}K,h_{C})\geqslant 0$ for any $C\in\mathcal{K}^{\dim E}_{s}$ . Therefore, by induction hypothesis, $\Delta(P_{I_{\ell}^{\perp}}(K+I_{1}+\cdots+I_{\ell}),h_{L})\geqslant 0$ holds for all $L\in\mathcal{K}^{n-1}_{s}$ . This allows us to apply Lemma 3.1 with $K\leftarrow K+I_{1}+\cdots+I_{\ell}$ , $I\leftarrow I_{\ell}$ , and $f\leftarrow f$ , which yields

$$ \Delta(K+I_{1}+\cdots+I_{\ell},f)\geqslant\Delta(K+I_{1}+\cdots+I_{\ell-1},\bar{f}) $$

for some $\bar{f}=f-c_{\ell}h_{K+I_{1}+\cdots+I_{\ell}}$ with $c_{\ell}\in{\mathbb{R}}$ . We may repeat this process $\ell$ times to obtain

$$ \Delta(K+I_{1}+\cdots+I_{\ell},f)\geqslant\Delta(K+I_{1}+\cdots+I_{\ell-1},\bar{f})\geqslant\cdots\geqslant\Delta(K,\tilde{f}), $$

where $\tilde{f}=f-c_{\ell}h_{K+I_{1}+\cdots+I_{\ell}}-\cdots-c_{1}h_{K+I_{1}}$ . Since $\Delta(K,\tilde{f})\geqslant 0$ by assumption, we have

$$ \Delta(K+I_{1}+\cdots+I_{\ell},f)\geqslant 0. $$

We have therefore shown that the sum of $K$ with any zonotope satisfies LLBM. Since zonoids are limits of zonotopes and mixed volumes are continuous with respect to Hausdorff convergence [11, Thm.5.1.7], $D(K+Z,f)\geqslant 0$ follows for any origin symmetric zonoid $Z$ and any $f\in D_{s}(S^{n-1})$ , which completes the proof. ∎

### 3.2. New proof for zonoids

Since we prove by induction on the dimension, it is necessary to check the base case.

#### Lemma 3.2.

Let $K\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}$ be a 1-dimensional origin symmetric zonotope, and let $f\in D_{s}(S^{0})$ . Then $\Delta(K,f)=0$ .

#### Proof.

Indeed, $K$ is of the form $K=[-a,a]$ for some $a>0$ . Hence $\Delta(K,f)=\frac{(f(1)+f(-1))^{2}}{2a}-\left(\frac{f(1)^{2}}{a}+\frac{f(-1)^{2}}{a}\right)=0$ because $f(1)=f(-1)$ . ∎

For a fixed dimension, in order to apply the induction on number of interval summands (Lemma 3.1), we just need to check that LLBM holds for the cube, which is a well-known fact. Nevertheless, we provide a proof which is based on formula (1) for sake of self-completeness.

#### Lemma 3.3.

Let $C$ be the cube $[-1,1]^{n}$ and $f\in D_{s}(S^{n-1})$ ( $n\geqslant 2$ ). Then $\Delta(C,f)\geqslant 0$ holds.

#### Proof.

Let $J=\{0\}^{n-1}\times[-1,1]$ . Fix $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ . Now apply Lemma 3.1 to $K=C$ and $I=(1-\varepsilon)J$ . We have $\Delta(C,f)\geqslant\Delta(C\div(1-\varepsilon)J,\bar{f})$ for $\bar{f}=f-ch_{C}$ where

$$ c=n\frac{V(C[n-1],f)}{V(C)}-(n-1)\frac{V(C[n-2],J,f)}{V(C[n-1],J)}. $$

Note that $\bar{f}$ is independent of $\varepsilon$ . Let us give the explicit value of $c$ . Let $C_{t}=C\div J+tJ$ for $t\in[0,1]$ . Note that $C_{0}=[-1,1]^{n-1}\times\{0\}=P_{J^{\perp}}C$ has zero volume. We have

$$ \displaystyle c= \displaystyle n\frac{V(C_{0}[n-1],f)-(n-1)V(C_{0}[n-2],J,f)}{nV(C_{0}[n-1],J)}+(n-1)\frac{V(C_{0}[n-2],J,f)}{V(C_{0}[n-1],J)} \displaystyle\quad=\frac{V(C_{0}[n-1],f)}{V(C_{0}[n-1],J)}, $$

where we used $V(J,J,\cdot,\dots,\cdot)=0$ . Since $C_{0}$ is a $n-1$ dimensional cube, we have $V(C_{0}[n-1],f)=\frac{2^{n-1}}{n}(f(e_{n})+f(-e_{n}))=\frac{2^{n}}{n}f(e_{n})$ and $V(C_{0}[n-1],J)=\frac{2^{n}}{n}$ . Hence $c=f(e_{n})$ . Therefore, $\bar{f}(-e_{n})=\bar{f}(e_{n})=f(e_{n})-ch_{C}(e_{n})=0$ . It follows that $V(C_{0}[n-1],\bar{f})=0$ . Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\Delta(C_{\varepsilon},\bar{f})= \displaystyle\frac{V(C_{\varepsilon}[n-1],\bar{f})^{2}}{V(C_{\varepsilon})}-\frac{n-1}{n}V(C_{\varepsilon}[n-2],\bar{f},\bar{f})-\frac{1}{n}V(C_{\varepsilon}[n-1],\tfrac{\bar{f}^{2}}{h_{C_{\varepsilon}}}) \displaystyle\geqslant \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\frac{V(C_{\varepsilon}[n-1],\bar{f})^{2}}{V(C_{\varepsilon})}-\frac{1}{n}V(C_{\varepsilon}[n-1],\tfrac{\bar{f}^{2}}{h_{C_{\varepsilon}}}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}\frac{(V(C_{0}[n-1],\bar{f})+(n-1)\varepsilon V(C_{0}[n-2],J,\bar{f}))^{2}}{V(C_{0})+n\varepsilon V(C_{0}[n-1],J)}-\frac{1}{n}V(C_{\varepsilon}[n-1],\tfrac{\bar{f}^{2}}{h_{C_{\varepsilon}}}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\varepsilon\frac{(n-1)^{2}V(C_{0}[n-2],J,\bar{f})^{2}}{n^{2}V(C_{0}[n-1],J)}-\frac{1}{n}V(C_{\varepsilon}[n-1],\tfrac{\bar{f}^{2}}{h_{C_{\varepsilon}}}), $$

where we used the Alexandrov-Fenchel inequality and expanded the mixed volumes involving $C_{\varepsilon}=C_{0}+\varepsilon J$ . Therefore,

$$ \liminf_{\varepsilon\to 0}\Delta(C_{\varepsilon},\bar{f})\geqslant-\limsup_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{1}{n}V(C_{\varepsilon}[n-1],\tfrac{\bar{f}^{2}}{h_{C_{\varepsilon}}})=0 $$

because $\bar{f}(\pm e_{n})=0$ . By Lemma 3.1, $\Delta(C,f)\geqslant\liminf_{\varepsilon\to 0}\Delta(C_{\varepsilon},\bar{f})\geqslant 0$ , which completes the proof.

∎

#### Proposition 3.4.

Assume $D(K,f)\geqslant 0$ holds for all zonotopes $K\in\mathcal{K}^{n-1}_{s}$ and $f\in D_{s}(S^{n-2})$ ( $n\geqslant 2$ ). Then $D(K,f)\geqslant 0$ holds for all zonotopes $K\in\mathcal{K}^{n}_{s}$ and $f\in D_{s}(S^{n-1})$ .

#### Proof.

Let $K=I_{1}+\cdots+I_{\ell}$ with $I_{j}$ being origin symmetric segments with distinct directions. We induct on the value of $\ell$ . Since $K$ is $n$ -dimensional, $\ell\geqslant n$ .

For the base case $\ell=n$ , $K=A(C)$ for some non-degenerate linear transform $A$ , where $C=[-1,1]^{n}$ . We have $\Delta(K,f)=\Delta(A(C),f)=|\det(A)|\Delta(C,f\circ A^{-t})\geqslant 0$ by (4) and Lemma 3.3.

Assume the conclusion is proved for $\ell-1$ , let’s prove it for $\ell$ . Since $P_{I_{\ell}^{\perp}}K\in\mathcal{K}^{n-1}_{s}$ is a zonotope, by hypothesis we have $\Delta(P_{I_{\ell}^{\perp}}K,g)\geqslant 0$ for all $g\in D_{s}(S^{n-2})$ . This allows us to apply Lemma 3.1 to $K$ and $I_{\ell}$ , obtaining $\Delta(K,f)\geqslant\Delta(K\div I_{\ell},\bar{f})$ for some $\bar{f}\in D_{s}(S^{n-1})$ . By the induction hypothesis for $\ell-1$ , $\Delta(K\div I_{\ell},\bar{f})\geqslant 0$ since $\bar{f}\in D_{s}(S^{n-1})$ . Therefore $\Delta(K,f)\geqslant 0$ holds as desired. ∎

#### Theorem 3.5.

$\Delta(K,f)\geqslant 0$ holds for all zonoids $K\in\mathcal{K}^{n}_{s}$ and all $f\in D_{s}(S^{n-1})$ .

#### Proof.

By a standard approximation argument, it suffices to prove the claim for zonotopes $K\in\mathcal{K}^{n}_{s}$ . We induct on the dimension $n$ . The case $n=1$ is dealt with in Lemma 3.2 and the induction step is given by Proposition 3.4, which completes the proof. ∎

## 4. Equality cases for smooth bodies with $C^{2}$ support functions

In this section, we will assume the LLBM inequality is true and study the equality cases of LLBM for smooth bodies with $C^{2}$ support functions. It turns out that the monotonicity principle proved in Theorem 1.2 can be adapted to prove that only trivial equality cases appear in this case.

### 4.1.

Recall that a convex body is called smooth if all of its boundary points have a unique unit normal vector. For two convex bodies $K$ , $L$ , denote the Minkowski subtraction by $K\div L:=\{x\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\mid L+x\subseteq K\}$ . The following fact is a strengthening of [11, Lemma 7.5.4]. Schneider’s original statement didn’t involve the uniform convergence part, which will be necessary in the proof of Proposition 4.5. Note also that Fact 4.2 only assumes $K$ is full dimensional but not $L$ , which is the case we need. The proof of Fact 4.2 follows principally the same lines as Schneider’s proof.

#### Definition 4.1.

For two convex bodies $K,L$ , we say that $L$ is adapted to $K$ if for every $x\in\partial K$ there exists $y\in\partial L$ such that $N(K,x)\subseteq N(L,y)$ .

Note that if $K$ is smooth, then any body $L$ is adapted to $K$ .

#### Fact 4.2.

Let $K,L\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ be convex bodies. Assume $K$ is full dimensional and $L$ is adapted to $K$ . Let

$$ K_{t}:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}K+tL,&t\geqslant 0,\\
K\div(-t)L,&t<0.\end{array}\right. $$

Then

$$ \lim_{t\to 0}\left\|\frac{h_{K_{t}}-h_{K}}{t}-h_{L}\right\|_{L^{\infty}(S^{n-1})}=0. $$

In particular,

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}h_{K_{t}}=h_{L}. $$

#### Proof.

Since $h_{K_{t}}=h_{K}+th_{L}$ for $t\geqslant 0$ , the desired conclusion is obvious for $t\rightarrow 0+$ . Therefore, in the following we only consider the limit $t\to 0-$ .

Step 1: Let $u\in S^{n-1}$ . For all small $t>0$ such that $K\div tL\neq\emptyset$ , take $z\in F(K\div tL,u)$ . Let

$$ U_{t}(u):=\{v\in S^{n-1}\mid h_{K}(v)=h_{tL+z}(v)\}. $$

We claim that

$$ u\in\operatorname{pos}U_{t}(u):=\Bigr\{\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}\lambda_{i}v_{i}:\lambda_{i}\geqslant 0,\,v_{i}\in U_{t}(u),\ell\in{\mathbb{N}}\Bigr\}. $$

Indeed, if this were false, then $\operatorname{pos}U_{t}(u)\setminus\{0\}$ and $u$ are separated by a hyperplane. That is, there exists $w\in{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ such that $\langle w,u\rangle>0$ and $\langle w,v\rangle<0$ for all $v\in U_{t}(u)\setminus\{0\}$ . Therefore, $h_{K}-h_{tL+z}$ is positive on $S^{n-1}\cap\{x:\langle x,w\rangle\geqslant 0\}$ . In particular, there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that

$$ h_{K}(v)-h_{tL+z}(v)\geqslant\varepsilon\langle w,v\rangle $$

holds for all $v\in S^{n-1}$ . This implies $tL+z+\varepsilon w\subseteq K$ . Hence $z+\varepsilon w\in K\div tL$ . However, $\langle z+\varepsilon w,u\rangle>\langle z,u\rangle$ . A contradiction to the choice of $z$ .

Step 2: By (9) and Carathéodory’s theorem, we may choose $v_{1},...,v_{n}\in U_{t}(u)$ and $\lambda_{1},...,\lambda_{n}\geqslant 0$ such that $u=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}v_{i}$ . We have

$$ \displaystyle\frac{h_{K}(u)-h_{K\div tL}(u)}{t}-h_{L}(u)=\frac{h_{K}(u)-h_{K\div tL+tL}(u)}{t} \displaystyle\qquad\leqslant\frac{h_{K}(u)-h_{z+tL}(u)}{t}\leqslant\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}h_{K}(v_{i})-h_{z+tL}(u)}{t} \displaystyle\qquad=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}h_{z+tL}(v_{i})-h_{z+tL}(u)}{t}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}h_{L}(v_{i})-h_{L}(u), $$

where for the first inequality we used $z\in K\div tL$ and for the second inequality the convexity of support functions. Combine this with the fact that $K\supseteq K\div tL+tL$ , we obtain

$$ 0\leqslant\frac{h_{K}(u)-h_{K\div tL}(u)}{t}-h_{L}(u)\leqslant\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}h_{L}(v_{i})-h_{L}(u). $$

Step 3: We claim that (note that both $\lambda_{i}$ and $v_{i}$ depend on $u$ )

$$ \lim_{t\to 0}\sup_{u\in S^{n-1}}\Bigr|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}h_{L}(v_{i})-h_{L}(u)\Bigr|=0. $$

Assume the converse. Then there exists a number $\alpha>0$ , a sequence $(t_{j})_{i=1}^{\infty}$ converging to $0$ , a sequence $(u_{j})_{i=1}^{\infty}$ in $S^{n-1}$ , a sequence $(z_{j})_{i=1}^{\infty}$ , sequences $(v_{i,j})_{i=1}^{\infty}$ , $i=1,...,n$ , and sequences of positive numbers $(\lambda_{i,j})_{1\leqslant i\leqslant n,1\leqslant j<\infty}$ , such that

$$ \displaystyle z_{j}\in F(K\div t_{j}L,u_{j}),\quad v_{i,j}\in U_{t_{j}}(u_{j})=\{v\in S^{n-1}:h_{K}(v)=h_{t_{j}L+z_{j}}(v)\} \displaystyle u_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i,j}v_{i,j},\quad\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i,j}h_{L}(v_{i,j})-h_{L}(u_{j})>\alpha. $$

Up to passing to a subsequence, we may assume $u_{j}$ converges to $u\in S^{n-1}$ , $z_{j}$ converges to $z\in F(K,u)$ , and $v_{i,j}$ converges to $v_{i}$ for every $i$ . From $v_{i,j}\in U_{t_{j}}(u_{j})$ we have $h_{K}(v_{i})=h_{z}(v_{i})$ . Hence $v_{i}\in N(K,z)$ .

By applying Blaschke selection theorem to $\operatorname{pos}(U_{t_{j}}(u_{j}))\cap S^{n-1}$ we may assume that after passing to a subsequence, $\operatorname{pos}(U_{t_{j}}(u_{j}))\cap S^{n-1}$ converges to $P\cap S^{n-1}$ , where $P$ is a closed convex cone.

We claim $P$ does not contain any lineality space. Indeed, assume this is not true, then there exist $\ell\in[n]$ and sequences $(w_{j}^{k})_{1\leqslant j<\infty}$ for $1\leqslant k\leqslant\ell$ , such that $w_{j}^{k}\in U_{t_{j}}(u_{j})$ , $\lim_{j\to\infty}w_{j}^{k}=w^{k}$ , and $\operatorname{pos}(w^{k},k\in[\ell])$ is equal to the lineality space of $P$ . However, from $w_{j}^{k}\in U_{t_{j}}(u_{j})$ we have $h_{K}(w_{j}^{k})=h_{t_{j}L+z_{j}}(w_{j}^{k})$ . Letting $j$ tend to infinity we obtain $h_{K}(w^{k})=\langle z,w^{k}\rangle$ , i.e., $w^{k}\in N(K,z)$ . This is a contradiction since $N(K,u)$ does not contain any lineality space due to the full dimensionality assumption on $K$ .

By our previous claim, there exists $b\in S^{n-1}$ and $\delta>0$ such that $P\subseteq\{v:\langle b,v\rangle\geqslant\delta\|v\|\}$ . Using this and $u_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i,j}v_{i,j}$ , we obtain that for sufficiently large $j$ ,

$$ 1\geqslant\langle b,u_{j}\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i,j}\langle b,v_{i,j}\rangle\geqslant\delta/2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i,j}. $$

Therefore, $\lambda_{i,j}$ are uniformly bounded and we may assume $\lim_{j\to\infty}\lambda_{i,j}=\lambda_{i}$ by passing to a subsequence. By (11) we have

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}h_{L}(v_{i})-h_{L}(u)>\alpha. $$

On the other hand, by adaptedness we obtain that there exists $y\in\partial L$ such that $N(K,z)\subseteq N(L,y)$ . Since $z\in F(K,u)$ and $v_{i}\in N(K,z)$ holds for all $i$ , we have $u,v_{1},...,v_{n}\in N(L,y)$ . Hence $\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}h_{L}(v_{i})-h_{L}(u)=0$ , a contradiction.

∎

Another fact we will use follows from the case $m=n-1$ of [11, Theorem 4.5.3].

#### Fact 4.3.

Let $K$ be a smooth body, then the support of its area measure $S_{K}$ is $S^{n-1}$ .

We recall lastly a standard measure theory fact.

#### Lemma 4.4.

Let $\mu_{i}$ be a sequence of Borel measures on $S^{n-1}$ and $f_{n}$ a sequence of functions. Assume $\mu_{i}$ converges weakly to a finite measure $\mu$ and $f_{i}$ converges uniformly to a continuous function $f$ . Then $\int_{S^{n-1}}f_{i}d\mu_{i}$ converges to $\int_{S^{n-1}}fd\mu$ .

#### Proof.

Indeed,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{i\to\infty}\Bigr| \displaystyle\int_{S^{n-1}}f_{i}d\mu_{i}-\int_{S^{n-1}}fd\mu\Bigr| \displaystyle\leqslant\limsup_{i\to\infty}\Bigr|\int_{S^{n-1}}f_{i}-fd\mu_{i}\Bigr|+\limsup_{i\to\infty}\Bigr|\int_{S^{n-1}}fd\mu_{i}-\int_{S^{n-1}}fd\mu\Bigr| \displaystyle\leqslant\limsup_{i\to\infty}\|f_{i}-f\|_{L^{\infty}(S^{n-1})}\mu_{i}(S^{n-1})=0, $$

where we used the weak convergence of $\mu_{i}$ to $\mu$ in the second inequality.

∎

### 4.2.

We are now ready to state the analogous equation to (1) for parallel bodies $(K_{t})_{t}$ obtained from $K$ and a segment $I$ .

#### Proposition 4.5.

Let $K\subseteq{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ be a smooth body containing the origin in its interior such that $h_{K}|_{S^{n-1}}$ is $C^{2}$ . Let $I$ be an origin-symmetric segment. Define $K_{t}=K+tI$ for $t>0$ and $K_{t}=K\div(-t)I$ for $t\leqslant 0$ . Let $f$ be a $C^{2}$ function on $S^{n-1}$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0} \displaystyle\Delta(K_{t},f) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{(n-1)^{2}}{n}\left(\frac{V(K[n-2],I,f)^{2}}{V(K[n-1],I)}-\frac{n-2}{n-1}V(K[n-3],I,f,f)-\frac{1}{n-1}V(K[n-2],I,\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}})\right) \displaystyle-nV(K[n-1],I)\left(\frac{V(K[n-1],f)}{V(K)}-\frac{n-1}{n}\frac{V(K[n-2],I,f)}{V(K[n-1],I)}\right)^{2} \displaystyle+\frac{1}{n}V(K[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}^{2}}h_{I}). $$

#### Proof.

The formal algebraic computation is the same as (1). Hence it remains to justify the interchange of mixed volume with taking derivatives.

Step 1: In this step we show $\frac{d}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}V(K_{t})=nV(K[n-1],I)$ . We have,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}V(K_{t})= \displaystyle\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{V(K_{t})-V(K)}{t} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\lim_{t\to 0}\sum_{i=1}^{n}V(K_{t}[n-i],K[i-1],\tfrac{h_{K_{t}}-h_{K}}{t}) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{n}\int_{S^{n-1}}\frac{h_{K_{t}}-h_{K}}{t}dS_{K_{t}[n-i],K[i-1]}. $$

By Fact 4.2, $\frac{h_{K_{t}}-h_{K}}{t}$ converges uniformly to $h_{I}$ . It follows that $K_{t}$ converges to $K$ in Hausdorff distance as $t$ converges to 0. Hence $S_{K_{t}[n-i],K[i-1]}$ weakly converges to $S_{K}$ [11, Page 281], which is a finite measure. By Lemma 4.4,

$$ \lim_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{n}\int_{S^{n-1}}\frac{h_{K_{t}}-h_{K}}{t}dS_{K_{t}[n-i],K[i-1]}=V(K[n-1],h_{I}). $$

Plug this back into (13), we obtain $\frac{d}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}V(K_{t})=nV(K[n-1],h_{I})$ as desired.

Since $f$ is $C^{2}$ , we may write $f=h_{L}-h_{M}$ for some convex bodies $L,M$ [12, Cor.2.2]. It is then clear that the above proof works verbatim for $\frac{d}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}V(K_{t}[n-1],f)=(n-1)V(K[n-2],I,f)$ and $\frac{d}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}V(K_{t}[n-2],f,f)=(n-2)V(K[n-3],I,f,f)$ .

Step 2: In this step we show

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}V(K_{t}[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K_{t}}})=(n-1)V(K[n-2],I,\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}})-V(K[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}^{2}}h_{I}). $$

Indeed we have,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{V(K_{t}[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K_{t}}})-V(K[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}})}{t} \displaystyle\quad=V(K_{t}[n-1],\tfrac{1}{t}(\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K_{t}}}-\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}}))+\tfrac{1}{t}(V(K_{t}[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}})-V(K[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}})). $$

On the one hand, we have $\tfrac{1}{t}(\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K_{t}}}-\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}})=-\frac{f^{2}}{h_{K}h_{K_{t}}}\frac{h_{K_{t}}-h_{K}}{t}$ . Since $\frac{h_{K_{t}}-h_{K}}{t}$ converges uniformly to $h_{I}$ as $t$ goes to $0$ by Fact 4.2, we know $\tfrac{1}{t}(\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K_{t}}}-\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}})$ converges uniformly to $-\frac{f^{2}}{h_{K}^{2}}h_{I}$ . Also $S_{K_{t}}$ converges weakly to $S_{K}$ . By Lemma 4.4,

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{t\to 0}V( \displaystyle K_{t}[n-1],\tfrac{1}{t}(\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K_{t}}}-\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}}))=-V(K[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}^{2}}h_{I}), $$

On the other hand, since $f$ and $h_{K}$ are $C^{2}$ functions and $K$ contains the origin in its interior, $\frac{f^{2}}{h_{K}}$ also is a $C^{2}$ function. Therefore, it is possible to find two convex bodies $L,M$ such that $\frac{f^{2}}{h_{K}}=h_{L}-h_{M}$ [12, Cor.2.2]. We can again run the exact same argument as in Step 1 to obtain

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{t\to 0}\tfrac{1}{t} \displaystyle(V(K_{t}[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}})-V(K[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}})) \displaystyle=\lim_{t\to 0}\bigr[\tfrac{1}{t}(V(K_{t}[n-1],L)-V(K[n-1],L))-\tfrac{1}{t}(V(K_{t}[n-1],M)-V(K[n-1],M))\bigr] \displaystyle=(n-1)V(K[n-2],I,L)-(n-1)V(K[n-2],I,M) \displaystyle=(n-1)V(K[n-2],I,\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}}). $$

Combine this with (15), we obtain (14).

∎

#### Proof of Theorem 1.3.

Let $f=h_{L}-ch_{K}$ where

$$ c=n\frac{V(K[n-1],L)}{V(K)}-(n-1)\frac{V(K[n-2],I,L)}{V(K[n-1],I)}. $$

From the choice of $c$ , it follows that

$$ \frac{V(K[n-1],f)}{V(K)}-\frac{n-1}{n}\frac{V(K[n-2],I,f)}{V(K[n-1],I)}=0 $$

Fix any origin-symmetric segment $I$ . Let

$$ K_{t}:=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}K+tI,&t\geqslant 0,\\
K\div(-t)I,&t<0.\end{array}\right. $$

Since $K$ is smooth, $I$ is adapted to $K$ . Using Fact 4.2, $\frac{d}{dt}\bigr|_{t=0}h_{K_{t}}=h_{I}$ . By Proposition 4.5,

$$ \displaystyle\frac{d}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0} \displaystyle\Delta(K_{t},f) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{(n-1)^{2}}{n^{2}}|I|\Delta(P_{I^{\perp}}K,f|_{I^{\perp}})+\frac{1}{n}V(K[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}^{2}}h_{I}) \displaystyle-nV(K[n-1],I)\left(\frac{V(K[n-1],f)}{V(K)}-\frac{n-1}{n}\frac{V(K[n-2],I,f)}{V(K[n-1],I)}\right)^{2} \displaystyle\geqslant \displaystyle\frac{1}{n}V(K[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}^{2}}h_{I})\geqslant 0, $$

where for the first inequality we used the assumption that the local log-Brunn-Minkowski inequality is true and (16).

By the assumption on LLBM we have $\Delta(K_{t},f)\geqslant 0$ . But Lemma 1.1 implies $\Delta(K,f)=0$ . Hence $t=0$ minimizes $\Delta(K_{t},f)$ and we have

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\Bigr|_{t=0}\Delta(K_{t},f)=0. $$

Combine this with (17), we obtain $V(K[n-1],\tfrac{f^{2}}{h_{K}^{2}}h_{I})=0$ , which is

$$ \int_{S^{n-1}}\frac{f^{2}}{h_{K}^{2}}h_{I}dS_{K}=0. $$

Therefore,

$$ \frac{f^{2}}{h_{K}^{2}}h_{I}=0\text{ on }\operatorname{supp}S_{K}. $$

By Fact 4.3, $\operatorname{supp}S_{K}=S^{n-1}$ . Since $h_{I}(u)\neq 0$ holds for all $u\notin I^{\perp}$ , we have $f(u)=0$ for all $u\notin I^{\perp}\cap S^{n-1}$ . Since $f$ is continuous and $S^{n-1}\setminus I^{\perp}$ is dense in $S^{n-1}$ , we conclude that $f(u)=0$ for all $u\in S^{n-1}$ . Therefore, $h_{L}=ch_{K}+f=ch_{K}$ , which completes the proof.

# An identity in distribution between full-space and half-space log-gamma polymers

**Authors:** Guillaume Barraquand Address: G. Barraquand, Laboratoire de Physique de l’école normale supérieure, ENS, Université PSL, CNRS, Sorbonne Université, Université de Paris, Paris, France Email address: guillaume.barraquand@ens.fr and Shouda Wang Address: Shouda Wang, École Polytechnique, Institut Polytechnique de Paris, Route de Saclay, F-91120 Palaiseau Cedex, France and Laboratoire de Physique de l’école normale supérieure, ENS, Université PSL, CNRS, Sorbonne Université, Université de Paris, Paris, France Email address: shoudawang@princeton.edu

## Abstract

We prove an identity in distribution between two kinds of partition functions for the log-gamma directed polymer model: (1) the point-to-point partition function in a quadrant, (2) the point-to-line partition function in an octant. As an application, we prove that the point-to-line free energy of the log-gamma polymer in an octant obeys a phase transition depending on the strength of the noise along the boundary. This transition of (de)pinning by randomness was first predicted in physics by Kardar in 1985 and proved rigorously for zero temperature models by Baik and Rains in 2001. While it is expected to arise universally for models in the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality class, this is the first positive temperature model for which this transition can be rigorously established.

#### Contents

- 1 Introduction and main results

- 2 Geometric RSK correspondence and Whittaker functions

- 3 Laplace transform of the partition function for trapezoidal log-gamma polymers

- 4 Proof of Theorem

- 5 Asymptotics results for trapezoidal log-gamma polymers

- References

## 1. Introduction and main results

### 1.1. Preface

Models of directed polymers in $1+1$ dimensions confined to a half-space are expected to obey a phase transition depending on the strength of the noise along the boundary. This phenomenon was predicted in physics by Kardar in [Kar85] and termed depinning by quenched randomness. A more precise understanding of this transition came from the study of specific exactly solvable models by Baik and Rains [BR01a, BR01b]. When the strength of the disorder on the boundary is below a certain threshold, the asymptotic behaviour of the free energy is the same as without a boundary: fluctuations are governed by a one third scaling exponent and statistics related to random matrix theory, as usually for models in the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) universality class. Above this threshold, free energy fluctuations are Gaussian distributed on a square root scale, as if fluctuations were only determined by the noise along the boundary.

In order to establish these results, [BR01a] applied the RSK correspondence on random matrices satisfying various symmetries. For each symmetry type, they computed the exact distribution of the RSK shape in terms of Schur functions. This enabled them to study in particular an exactly solvable model of last passage percolation, i.e., a directed polymer at zero temperature, where the symmetry imposed on the weights of the model is equivalent to confining polymer paths in a half-space (an octant of the $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ lattice). The distribution of the free energy can then be characterized by determinantal and Pfaffian formulas, which can be asymptotically analyzed [BR01b].

All models studied in [BR01a, BR01b] (applications of [BR01a, BR01b] are reviewed in [BR01c]) can be considered as free-fermionic models. Positive temperature models are however typically not free-fermionic and arguably more difficult to study. Some of the results of Baik and Rains have been lifted to the positive temperature setting in [OSZ14, BZ19b, BBC20, BOZ21], using the geometric RSK correspondence instead of the usual one, and Whittaker functions instead of Schur functions. These works provide concise exact formulas for observables of interest of various models, but none of these formulas seem to be readily amenable for asymptotic analysis – see e.g. the discussion in [BBC20, Sections 1.4 and 8]. Thus, a proof of a depinning phase transition for a half-space polymer model at positive temperature, or any model in the KPZ class that is not free-fermionic, has remained out of reach.

In this paper, we consider the point-to-line partition function (and more generally the point-to-half-line partition function) for a log-gamma polymer model in an octant. We prove an identity in distribution between those partition functions and point-to-point partition functions in a quadrant. Relying on known asymptotics for the latter [BCR13, KQ18, BCD21], we prove that the point-to-line partition function in an octant obeys a phase transition, depending on the parameter of weights along the boundary. 11 1 We remark that earlier progresses towards a proof of this phase transition [OSZ14, BBC20] focused on the point-to-point partition function, which is expected to obey a similar phase transition with slightly different statistics. See predictions based on non-rigorous asymptotics in [BBC20]. The identity in distribution is valid for inhomogenous weights distributions, depending on two families of inhomogeneity parameters. The proof is based on applying the geometric RSK algorithm to symmetric random matrices with inverse-gamma distributed weights, and computing the distribution of observables of interest as integrals involving $\mathfrak{g}\mathfrak{l}_{n}(\mathbb{R})$ -Whittaker functions and their orthogonal analogues. This generalizes a similar computation in [BZ19b]. The identity in distribution between the two partition functions may finally be recognized after transforming formulas using the spectral theory associated with Whittaker functions and comparing the Laplace transform formula for the point-to-line partition function to the one for the point-to-point partition function [COSZ14].

### 1.2. The log-gamma polymer

Let us define the log-gamma directed polymer model, first introduced in [Sep12].

#### Definition 1.1 (Partition function of log-gamma polymers).

Let $\mathcal{I}\subset\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ be an index set. Let $(\theta_{i,j})_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}}$ be a parameter array with positive entries $\theta_{i,j}>0$ for all $(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}$ . We define the weight array of the log-gamma polymer with index set $\mathcal{I}$ and parameter array $(\theta_{i,j})$ as a family of independent inverse-gamma random variables $(W_{i,j})_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}}$ such that $W_{i,j}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}^{-1}(\theta_{i,j})$ (equivalently $W_{i,j}^{-1}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\theta_{i,j})$ ) for $(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}$ . More precisely, the density function of $W_{i,j}$ is given by

$$ f_{W_{i,j}}(x)=\frac{1}{\Gamma(\theta_{i,j})}x^{-\theta_{i,j}-1}e^{-\frac{1}{x}},\quad\text{for}\quad x>0. $$

Suppose that $(1,1)$ and $(n,N)\in\mathcal{I}$ . We define the (point-to-point) partition function of the log-gamma polymer via

$$ {Z(n,N)}=\sum_{\pi:(1,1)\to(n,N)}\prod_{(i,j)\in\pi}W_{i,j}. $$

where the sum is over all up-right paths from $(1,1)$ to $(n,N)$ confined in $\mathcal{I}$ . See Figure 1. We are particularly interested in the following two types of domains of $\mathbb{Z}^{2}$ and their corresponding index set:

- (i) Rectangular domains, with index set $\mathcal{I}=\{(i,j)\mid 1\leqslant i\leqslant n,1\leqslant j\leqslant m\}$ for some $n,m$ , will be used to define full-space point-to-point partition functions as (1.1).

- (ii) Trapezoidal domains, where in particular the paths are confined inside an octant, with index set $\mathcal{I}=\{(i,j)\mid 1\leqslant i\leqslant n,i\leqslant j\leqslant 2n+m-i+1\}$ for some $n,m$ , will be used to define trapezoidal point-to-line partition functions.

#### Remark 1.7.

The equality between (1.6) and (1.7) (which holds for any $m\geqslant 0$ ) is a sign of – seemingly unknown – properties of Whittaker functions. For $m=0$ , the identity reads

$$ r^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}}\int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}}e^{-r/x_{n}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i}/r)^{(-1)^{i}}\right)^{\alpha_{\circ}}\Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{o}_{2n+1}}(\bm{x})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\tfrac{{d}x_{i}}{x_{i}}=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}}e^{-rx_{1}}\Psi^{\mathfrak{g}\mathfrak{l}_{n}}_{\alpha_{\circ}\sqcup\bm{\alpha};1}(\bm{x})\Psi^{\mathfrak{g}\mathfrak{l}_{n}}_{\bm{\alpha}}(\bm{x})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\tfrac{dx_{i}}{x_{i}}. $$

An analogous identity holds in the zero temperature limit, where one considers geometric last passage percolation instead of the log-gamma polymer. This identity was obtained in [BR01a, (7.59), (7.60)] (see also [BZ19b, Section 4] and [BZ19a]). Integrals in (1.6) and (1.7) become sums over integer partitions in [BR01a] and Whittaker functions become Schur functions. Another combinatorial proof of (a special case) of this identity at the Schur function level was proposed in [BZ19c], using generalizations of bounded Littlewood identities from [Ste90, Mac95, Oka98, Kra98]. Bounded Littlewood identities also appear in [Bet18] in a very similar context. It would be interesting to investigate whether the properties of Schur functions used in [Bet18, BZ19c] may be generalized to Macdonald polynomials and Whittaker functions (see [RW21] for partial answers).

### 1.4. Asymptotics

Many asymptotic results have been obtained for partition functions of full-space directed polymer models [ACQ11, SS10, CLDR10, Dot10, BC14, BCF14, BCFV15, IS17, AKQ14], and in particular for the log-gamma polymer [BCR13, KQ18, BCD21]. Yet not many rigorous asymptotic results exist for models in half-space. Theorem 1.4 bridges asymptotics in the full-space case to the half-space case (and more generally, the trapezoidal case). Before stating our asymptotic result, let us fix some notations.

#### Definition 1.8.

Suppose $\theta,\delta>0$ are fixed constants. Suppose $n$ and $m\geqslant n$ are integers that tend to infinity in such a way that $\frac{n}{m}>\delta$ holds. We denote $\frac{m}{n}$ by $p$ in the sequel. We assume that $n$ is the variable that tends to infinity and $m,p$ are merely functions of $n$ . Now we need to introduce certain quantities appearing in the limit theorem below. Let $\psi$ denote the digamma function defined on $\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ by

$$ \psi(z)=\partial_{z}\log\Gamma(z)=-\gamma+\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{n+1}-\frac{1}{n+z}\right). $$

Here $\gamma$ is the Euler–Mascheroni constant. Its derivative $\psi^{\prime}(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(n+z)^{2}}$ is a strictly decreasing function.

#### Definition 1.9.

Fix $\theta>0$ . Define $\theta_{c}$ to be the unique solution to $\psi^{\prime}(\theta_{c})-p\psi^{\prime}(\theta-\theta_{c})=0$ . It is well-defined since $x\mapsto\psi^{\prime}(x)-p\psi^{\prime}(\theta-x)$ is a bijection from $(0,\theta)$ to $\mathbb{R}$ . Define

$$ f_{\theta,p}:=-\psi(\theta_{c})-p\psi(\theta-\theta_{c}),\,\,\text{ and }\bar{f}_{\theta,p}:=-\psi(\theta_{0})-p\psi(\theta-\theta_{0}). $$

Define also

$$ \sigma_{\theta,p}:=\left(\frac{-\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{c})-p\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta-\theta_{c})}{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{3}}. $$

Since $p$ depends on $n$ , the quantities $\theta_{c},f_{\theta,p},\bar{f}_{\theta,p},\sigma_{\theta,p}$ all depend on $n$ as well.

We prove Theorem 1.10 in Section 5. The part (2) of Theorem 1.10 is a direct consequence of [BCD21, Theorem 1.7], stated below in Proposition 5.2. The part (1) is deduced from [BCD21, Theorem 1.2, Theorem 1.7] via a coupling method. The part (3) is obtained using estimates from [Sep12] about stationary and homogeneous log-gamma polymer models.

An explanation for why the point-to-point partition function undergoes a phase transition under a perturbation of one column is provided in [BBAP05] (in the zero temperature limit). Recall that an inverse-gamma variable has large mean value when its parameter is small. For small enough values of $\theta_{0}$ , paths stay a macroscopic distance along the first column with large probability under the polymer measure, while for larger values of $\theta_{0}$ , paths would not be influenced by the different weights along the first column. We refer to [BBC20, Section 8.1] and [BCD21, Section 1.5] for a more detailed exposition of this argument in the context of the log-gamma polymer. In the half-space setting, a precise qualitative understanding of the measure on polymer paths, for various values of $\theta_{0}$ , is more difficult to obtain. Nevertheless, we expect that for a fixed $\theta_{0}<\theta_{c}$ , most paths under the polymer measure will hit the boundary a $\mathcal{O}(n)$ number of times, while when $\theta_{0}>\theta_{c}$ , the geometry of paths should be qualitatively similar as in the full-space case.

### 1.5. KPZ equation

The Kardar-Parisi-Zhang (KPZ) equation [KPZ86] is the stochastic PDE

$$ \partial_{t}h(t,x)=\tfrac{1}{2}\partial_{xx}h(t,x)+\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\partial_{x}h(t,x)\right)^{2}+\xi(t,x),\;\;x\in\mathbb{R},\,t>0, $$

where $\xi(t,x)$ is a space-time Gaussian white noise. By definition, we say that $h$ is a solution (in the Cole-Hopf sense) of (1.13) if $h(t,x)=\log\mathcal{Z}(t,x)$ where $\mathcal{Z}$ is a solution of the multiplicative noise stochastic heat equation (mSHE)

$$ \partial_{t}\mathcal{Z}(t,x)=\tfrac{1}{2}\partial_{x,x}\mathcal{Z}(t,x)+\mathcal{Z}(t,x)\xi(t,x),\;\;x\in\mathbb{R},\,t>0, $$

which can be given a precise meaning using Ito calculus, see for example the review [Cor12]. We also consider the KPZ equation on the half-line $\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0}$ . The solution depends on a boundary parameter which we will denote by $A\in\mathbb{R}$ . As is the case for the full-line KPZ equation, a solution of the KPZ equation on a half-line is defined as the logarithm of the mSHE on $\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0}$ with Robin type boundary condition

$$ \begin{cases}\partial_{t}\mathcal{Z}_{A}(t,x)=\tfrac{1}{2}\partial_{x,x}\mathcal{Z}_{A}(t,x)+\mathcal{Z}_{A}(t,x)\xi(t,x),\;\;x\in\mathbb{R}_{\geqslant 0},\,t>0,\\
\partial_{x}\mathcal{Z}_{A}(t,x)\big|_{x=0}=A\mathcal{Z}_{A}(t,0).\end{cases} $$

Since the solution $\mathcal{Z}_{A}(t,x)$ is not differentiable in $x$ , the boundary condition $\partial_{x}\mathcal{Z}_{A}(t,x)\big|_{x=0}=A\mathcal{Z}_{A}(t,0)$ cannot be enforced on the solution itself. It must be enforced on the half-line heat kernel used to define mild solutions, we refer to [CS18, Def. 2.5] for details.

It is predicted in the physics paper [BLD21] that for all $t>0$ , $X\geqslant 0$ and $A\in\mathbb{R}$ , the identity in distribution

$$ \mathcal{Z}_{A}(t,0)=2\mathcal{Z}(t,-X) $$

holds, where, in the LHS, $\mathcal{Z}_{A}$ is the solution to (1.15) with initial data $\mathcal{Z}_{A}(0,x)=\mathbf{1}_{x\geqslant X}$ , and in the RHS, $\mathcal{Z}$ is the solution to (1.14) with initial data $\mathcal{Z}(0,x)=\mathbf{1}_{x\geqslant 0}\,e^{B_{x}-(A+\frac{1}{2})x}$ , where $B_{x}$ is a standard Brownian motion independent of the white noise $\xi$ . This prediction was based on the fact that moments of both sides of (1.16) match. However, this observation does not constitute a proof because moments of a solution to the mSHE do not uniquely determine its distribution.

We expect that (1.16) can be proved as a scaling limit of our main result (1.5). where the initial conditions are the same as those required for (1.16). The convergence of full-space directed polymer partition functions to the mSHE with delta initial data was first proved in [AKQ14]. The proof was extended to cover the particular setting of the log-gamma polymer in [CN17]. It seems however that the convergence stated in (1.18) is not proved in the existing literature, although the same initial condition was considered in [Par19] in a slightly different setting. Regarding half-space directed polymers, a general convergence result of the partition function of discrete polymer models to solutions of (1.15) was proved in [Wu20]. The result of [Wu20] applies to the log-gamma polymer, but only deals with point-to-point partition functions. It seems that significant extra work is needed to prove the convergence of the point-to-line partition function.

Thus, modulo the proof of convergences (1.18) and (1.19), our Theorem 1.4 implies (1.16). Proofs of these convergences are outside the scope of the present paper, but we hope that proving (1.16) may be a motivation to extend the existing proofs of convergence for full-space and half-space polymers to a more general setting, covering in particular (1.18) and (1.19).

### 1.6. Outline

In Section 2, we state and prove a number of prerequisites about the geometric RSK correspondence and Whittaker functions. In Section 3, we prove two formulas for the Laplace transform of the point-to-line partition function of trapezoidal log-gamma polymers. In Section 4, we prove the main identity in distribution (Theorem 1.4). In Section 5, we prove our asymptotic result (Theorem 1.10).

## 2. Geometric RSK correspondence and Whittaker functions

This section provides preliminary results useful in the following sections. In particular we introduce the geometric RSK correspondence (we will denote it by $\operatorname{gRSK}$ ) on polygonal arrays (in particular, symmetric polygonal arrays) and Whittaker functions. We refer the reader to Elia Bisi’s PhD thesis [Bis18] for a more detailed introduction to these subjects. We will also introduce the function $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha_{\circ},\bm{\beta};r}$ which appears in (1.6) and state some of its properties.

It was found in [OSZ14, COSZ14] that Whittaker functions arise naturally as we consider gRSK on (rectangular) domains (see also [O’C12] for an earlier occurrence of Whittaker functions in a directed polymer context). The partition functions for log-gamma polymers on such domains may be written as integrals involving Whittaker functions. For log-gamma polymers on non-rectangular domains, a generalization of gRSK to polygonal arrays [NZ17] may be used to derive, for example, the Laplace transform of the partition function, which is the approach adopted by [BZ19b] to treat half-space log-gamma polymers.

### 2.1. From half-space to symmetrized polymer partition functions

Before introducing gRSK, we point out that gRSK does not seem to apply well to trapezoidal domains, that we are interested in. However, a trapezoidal log-gamma polymer can always be converted to an equivalent symmetric log-gamma polymer, in that they have identical partition functions. And it is convenient to apply gRSK to symmetric domains [OSZ14, BZ19b].

### 2.2. Geometric RSK correspondence

The geometric RSK correspondence was introduced by Kirillov [Kir01] as the geometric lifting of the RSK correspondence. Noumi and Yamada proposed an alternative definition, purely written in terms of matrix algebra [NY04]. It is shown in [OSZ14] that gRSK can be constructed using local moves and that this is equivalent to [NY04]. In the following we present this construction via local moves.

#### 2.2.1. Geometric RSK correspondence on polygonal arrays

We start with some definitions.

#### Definition 2.1.

A polygonal domain $\mathcal{I}$ is a finite subset of $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ such that we have $(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}$ whenever $(i+1,j)\in\mathcal{I}$ or $(i,j+1)\in\mathcal{I}$ . A polygonal array on $\mathcal{I}$ is an array $(w_{p,q})_{(p,q)\in\mathcal{I}}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{|\mathcal{I}|}$ with positive entries indexed by a polygonal domain $\mathcal{I}$ . For notational convenience, we freely write $\bm{w}$ , $\bm{w}_{\mathcal{I}}$ , $(w_{p,q})$ , or $(w_{p,q})_{\mathcal{I}}$ to refer to the same polygonal array when there is no ambiguity.

An index $(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}$ is called a border index if $(i+1,j+1)$ does not belong to $\mathcal{I}$ . If none of $(i+1,j)$ , $(i,j+1)$ , $(i+1,j+1)$ belongs to $\mathcal{I}$ , then $(i,j)$ is called an outer index.

The gRSK map is a birational map between polygonal arrays on a same polygonal domain. The following presentation of gRSK, following [NZ17, OSZ14], is based on local moves. Local moves are birational maps between polygonal arrays that are localized on an entry and its neighbors. We will use two families of local moves $(a_{i,j})$ and $(b_{i,j})$ .

#### Definition 2.2.

Let $(w_{i,j})$ be a polygonal array on $\mathcal{I}$ . For an index $(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}$ , the local move $a_{i,j}$ replaces $w_{i,j}$ with

$$ w_{i,j}\left(w_{i-1,j}+w_{i,j-1}\right), $$

with the convention $w_{i,0}=w_{0,j}=0$ and $w_{0,1}+w_{1,0}=1$ . For a non-border index $(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}$ , the local move $b_{i,j}$ replaces $w_{i,j}$ with

$$ {w_{i,j}^{-1}}\left(w_{i-1,j}+w_{i,j-1}\right)\left({w_{i+1,j}}^{-1}+{w_{i,j+1}}^{-1}\right)^{-1}. $$

For $i\leqslant j$ ( $i\geqslant j$ resp.), let

$$ \varrho_{i,j}:=a_{i,j}\circ b_{i-1,j-1}\circ\dots\circ b_{1,j-i+1}\quad\left(\varrho_{i,j}:=a_{i,j}\circ b_{i-1,j-1}\circ\dots\circ b_{i-j+1,1}\text{ resp.}\right). $$

Now we are ready to give the definition of gRSK, which is done by induction. Let $\bm{w}$ be a polygonal array on $\mathcal{I}$ , let $\mathcal{I}_{\text{out}}$ be the set of outer indices of $\mathcal{I}$ and let $\mathcal{I}^{\circ}:=\mathcal{I}\setminus\mathcal{I}_{\text{out}}$ . The induction starts from $\operatorname{gRSK}(\varnothing):=\varnothing$ . By introducing the notations $\bm{w}^{\circ}=\left\{w_{i,j}:(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}^{\circ}\right\},\bm{w}^{\text{out }}=\left\{w_{i,j}:(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}_{\text{out}}\right\}$ , the induction relation reads

$$ \operatorname{gRSK}(\bm{w}):=\bigcirc_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}_{\text{out }}}\varrho_{i,j}\left(\operatorname{gRSK}\left(\bm{w}^{\circ}\right)\sqcup\bm{w}^{\text{out }}\right), $$

where $\bigcirc$ denotes compositions of $\varrho_{i,j}$ ’s and $\sqcup$ denotes union of two arrays. Note that the order in which the $\varrho_{i,j}$ ’s for $(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}_{\text{out }}$ are composed is irrelevant (see [NZ17]).

#### Proposition 2.3 ([NZ17, Proposition 2.6, 2.7]).

Let $\bm{t}=\operatorname{gRSK}(\bm{w})$ .

- • The Jacobian of the gRSK in log-coordinates

$$ \left(\log w_{i,j}:(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}\right)\mapsto\left(\log t_{i,j}:(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}\right) $$

has absolute value 1.

- • With the convention $t_{0,j}=t_{i,0}=0$ for all $i,j$ , we have

$$ \sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{1}{w_{i,j}}=\frac{1}{t_{1,1}}+\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{t_{i-1,j}+t_{i,j-1}}{t_{i,j}}. $$

- • For any border index $(n,m)$ ,

$$ t_{n,m}=\sum_{\pi:(1,1)\rightarrow(n,m)}\prod_{(i,j)\in\pi}w_{i,j}, $$

where the sum is over up-right paths from $(1,1)$ to $(n,m)$ .

- • For any border index $(n,m)$ ,

$$ \prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=1}^{m}w_{i,j}=\tau_{m-n}, $$

where $\tau_{q}:=\prod_{j-i=q}t_{i,j}$ . In particular, for an outer index $(n,m)$ ,

$$ \prod_{i=1}^{n}w_{i,m}=\frac{\tau_{m-n}}{\tau_{m-n-1}}\quad\text{and}\quad\prod_{j=1}^{m}w_{n,j}=\frac{\tau_{m-n}}{\tau_{m-n+1}} $$

hold.

Note that $t_{n,m}$ , $(n,m)$ being a border index, can thus be regarded as a point-to-point partition function for a polymer with weight array $\bm{w}$ .

#### 2.2.2. Symmetric geometric RSK correspondence

As motivated by Subsection 2.1, we introduce gRSK for symmetric arrays, first considered in [OSZ14]. Suppose $\mathcal{I}\subset\{(i,j)\mid i\leqslant j\}$ and that $\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{I}^{t}$ is a polygonal domain. Then a symmetric array $\bm{w}$ on $\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{I}^{t}$ only has $|\mathcal{I}|$ free variables (say, the restriction of $\bm{w}$ to the quadrant $\{(i,j)\mid i\leqslant j\}$ ). Let $\bm{t}:=\operatorname{gRSK}(\bm{w})$ , then $\bm{t}$ also is symmetric (see Proposition 2.4 below) and thus has $|\mathcal{I}|$ free variables. We may thus regard gRSK in this symmetric setting as a birational map from $\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{|\mathcal{I}|}$ to $\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{|\mathcal{I}|}$ .

#### Proposition 2.4 ([OSZ14, BZ19b]).

If $\bm{w}$ is symmetric, then $\bm{t}=\operatorname{gRSK}(\bm{w})$ is also symmetric. In addition, the Jacobian of

$$ \left(\log w_{i,j}:i\leqslant j\right)\mapsto\left(\log t_{i,j}:i\leqslant j\right) $$

has absolute value 1.

The following proposition provides a formula for the product of diagonal entries $\prod_{i}w_{i,i}$ in terms of $t_{j,j}$ ’s. This was first proved in [OSZ14, Lemma 5.1] for cases where the underlying polygonal domain is $\{(i,j)\mid 1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n\}$ for some $n$ . We provide a proof here for general symmetric polygonal arrays22 2 As pointed out by an anonymous referee, Proposition 2.5 can also be deduced from [OSZ14, Lemma 5.1] using the fact that the diagonal entries of the gRSK image of a polygonal array $\bm{w}$ coincide exactly with the diagonal entries of the gRSK image of the square subarray $\bm{w}^{sq}=(\bm{w}_{ij})_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant\ell}$ . In fact, this implies that Proposition 2.5 is still true under the weaker assumption that $\bm{w}^{sq}$ is symmetric..

We introduce the diagonal length $\ell$ of a polygonal array $\bm{w}$ on $\mathcal{I}$ as $\ell:=\operatorname{card}\{i\mid(i,i)\in\mathcal{I}\}$ .

#### Proposition 2.5.

Suppose $\bm{w}$ is a symmetric polygonal array. Let $\bm{t}=\operatorname{gRSK}(\bm{w})$ , then

$$ 4^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\prod_{i=1}^{n}w_{i,i}=\prod_{j=1}^{n}t_{j,j}^{(-1)^{n-j}}, $$

where $n$ is the diagonal length of $\bm{w}$ .

#### Proof.

We prove this by induction on $n$ . Observe that when $n=1$ , we have $\bm{t}=\bm{w}$ and the formula follows.

Suppose that the formula holds for any symmetric polygonal array of diagonal length $n-1$ , we now show that it also holds for any symmetric polygonal array $\bm{w}$ of diagonal length $n$ .

By (2.2), if $(n,n)$ is not an outer index, then $t^{\circ}_{j,j}=t_{j,j}$ for all $j=1,\dots,n$ , where $t^{\circ}$ denotes $\operatorname{gRSK}(\bm{w}^{\circ})$ . Since $w^{\circ}_{i,i}=w_{i,i}$ for all $1\leqslant i\leqslant n$ , the problem is thus reduced to proving the desired formula for $\bm{w}^{\circ}$ , which is $\bm{w}$ deprived of the entries on its outer indices. After repeating this process for a finite time, the reduction stops at some ${{{{\bm{w}^{\circ}}^{.}}^{.}}^{.}}^{\circ}$ , of which $(n,n)$ is an outer index (see Figure 4).

Assume now without loss of generality that $(n,n)$ is an outer index of $\bm{w}$ . Then the diagonal length of $\bm{w}^{\circ}$ is $n-1$ and the induction hypothesis yields

$$ 4^{\lfloor\tfrac{n-1}{2}\rfloor}\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}w_{ii}=\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}{t^{\circ}_{j,j}}^{(-1)^{n-1-j}}. $$

By the hypothesis that $\bm{w}$ is symmetric, $\bm{t}^{\circ}=\operatorname{gRSK}(\bm{w}^{\circ})$ is symmetric. Hence we may rewrite (2.2) as

$$ \displaystyle t_{1,1} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{t^{\circ}_{1,1}}\left(\frac{1}{t^{\circ}_{1,2}}+\frac{1}{t^{\circ}_{2,1}}\right)^{-1}=\frac{t^{\circ}_{1,2}}{2t^{\circ}_{1,1}}, \displaystyle t_{j,j} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{t^{\circ}_{j,j}}t^{\circ}_{j-1,j}t^{\circ}_{j,j+1},\quad\text{for}\quad 2\leqslant j\leqslant n-1, \displaystyle t_{n,n} \displaystyle=2w_{n,n}t_{n-1,n}^{\circ}. $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^{n}(t_{j,j})^{(-1)^{n-j}} \displaystyle=t_{n,n}{}t_{n-1,n-1}^{-1}{}t_{n-2,n-2}\cdots t_{1,1}^{(-1)^{n-1}} \displaystyle=2^{1+(-1)^{n}}w_{n,n}\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}(t_{j,j})^{(-1)^{n-1-j}} \displaystyle=2^{1+(-1)^{n}}w_{n,n}4^{\lfloor\tfrac{n-1}{2}\rfloor}\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}w_{i,i} \displaystyle=4^{\lfloor\tfrac{n}{2}\rfloor}\prod_{i=1}^{n}w_{i,i}, $$

which completes the proof.

### 2.3. Whittaker functions

We use $\mathrm{i}=\sqrt{-1}$ to denote the imaginary unit and reserve $i$ for use as indices.

#### 2.3.1. $\mathfrak{gl}_{n}$ -Whittaker functions

We define $\mathfrak{g}\mathfrak{l}_{n}$ -Whittaker functions through Givental’s integral formula [Giv97]. Fix a parameter sequence $\bm{\alpha}=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n})\in\mathbb{C}^{n}$ . Consider a triangular array $\bm{z}=(z_{i,j}:1\leqslant i\leqslant n,1\leqslant j\leqslant i)$ (Figure 5A). We define the type of such an array as

$$ \operatorname{type}(\bm{z})_{i}:=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^{i}z_{i,j}}{\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}z_{i-1,j}}\quad\text{ for }\quad i=1,\ldots,n, $$

with the convention $\prod_{j=1}^{0}z_{0,j}=1$ . Denote

$$ \operatorname{type}(\bm{z})^{\bm{\alpha}}:=\prod_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{type}(\bm{z})_{i}^{{\alpha}_{i}}. $$

The $\mathfrak{gl}_{n}$ -Whittaker function is defined via an integral on triangular arrays with fixed bottom row:

$$ \Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}}(\bm{x}):=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n(n-1)/2}}\operatorname{type}(\bm{z})^{-\bm{\alpha}}\exp\left(-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{i}\frac{z_{i+1,j+1}+z_{i-1,j}}{z_{i,j}}\right)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leqslant i<n\\
1\leqslant j\leqslant i\end{subarray}}\frac{dz_{i,j}}{z_{i,j}}, $$

where $z_{n,j}:=x_{j}$ for $1\leqslant j\leqslant n$ and by convention $z_{i,j}=0$ if $(i,j)$ is out of the range $1\leqslant i\leqslant n,1\leqslant j\leqslant i$ . A direct consequence of this definition is that for any $c\in\mathbb{C}$ ,

$$ \Psi_{\bm{\alpha}+c}^{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}}(\bm{x})=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\right)^{-c}\Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}}(\bm{x}). $$

*A $\mathfrak{gl}_{n}$ case, $n=6$ .*

*B $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}$ case, $n=3$ .*

*C generalized $\mathfrak{gl}_{n}$ case, $n=4,m=7$ .*

*Figure 5. Tableau of integral variables $z_{i,j}$ (including the fixed bottom row) for $\mathfrak{gl}_{n}$ Whittaker functions, $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}$ Whittaker functions, and generalized $\mathfrak{gl}_{n}$ -Whittaker functions; an arrow $a\rightarrow b$ means that the term $\frac{a}{b}$ appears in the exponential term in (2.3), (2.10), or (2.5), respectively for the three cases.*

Now we introduce a generalization of $\mathfrak{g}\mathfrak{l}_{n}$ -Whittaker functions, following [OSZ14]. This generalized Whittaker function will not be used in the sequel, but completes our discussion for (1.7). Suppose $m\geqslant n$ . Let $\bm{\beta}\in\mathbb{C}^{m}$ and let $r\in\mathbb{C}$ be such that $\Re(r)>0$ . Consider an array $\bm{z}=(z_{i,j}:1\leqslant i\leqslant m,1\leqslant j\leqslant i\wedge n)$ (Figure 5C). We define the type of such an array as

$$ \operatorname{type}(\bm{z})_{i}:=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^{i\wedge n}z_{i,j}}{\prod_{j=1}^{(i-1)\wedge n}z_{i-1,j}}\quad\text{ for }\quad i=1,\ldots,m. $$

Denote as above

$$ \operatorname{type}(\bm{z})^{\bm{\beta}}:=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{type}(\bm{z})_{i}^{{\beta}_{i}}. $$

The generalized $\mathfrak{gl}_{n}$ -Whittaker function is also defined via an integral on arrays with fixed bottom row:

$$ \Psi_{\bm{\beta};r}^{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}}(\bm{x}):=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{mn-n(n+1)/2}}\operatorname{type}(\bm{z})^{-\bm{\beta}}\exp\left(-\frac{r}{z_{n,n}}-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{i\wedge n}\frac{z_{i+1,j+1}+z_{i-1,j}}{z_{i,j}}\right)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leqslant i<m\\
1\leqslant j\leqslant i\wedge n\end{subarray}}\frac{dz_{i,j}}{z_{i,j}}, $$

where $z_{m,j}:=x_{j}$ for $1\leqslant j\leqslant n$ and by convention $z_{i,j}=0$ if $(i,j)$ is out of the range $1\leqslant i\leqslant m,1\leqslant j\leqslant i\wedge n$ .

For a function $g\in L^{2}\left(\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n},\prod_{i=1}^{n}{~d}x_{i}/x_{i}\right)$ , we define its Whittaker transform as

$$ \widehat{g}(\bm{\lambda}):=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}}g(\bm{x})\Psi_{\bm{\lambda}}^{\mathfrak{g}\mathfrak{l}_{n}}(\bm{x})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{dx_{i}}{x_{i}}. $$

Let $L_{\mathrm{sym}}^{2}\left((\mathrm{i}\mathbb{R})^{n},s_{n}(\bm{\lambda})d\bm{\lambda}\right)$ be the space of square integrable functions which are symmetric with respect to permuting their variables, equipped with the Sklyanin measure

$$ s_{n}(\bm{\lambda})=\frac{1}{(2\pi\mathrm{i})^{n}n!}\prod_{j\neq k}\Gamma\left(\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{k}\right)^{-1}. $$

It is known that the Whittaker transformation $g\mapsto\widehat{g}$ is an isometry from $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n},\prod_{i=1}^{n}dx_{i}/x_{i})$ to $L_{\mathrm{sym}}^{2}\left((\mathrm{i}\mathbb{R})^{n},s_{n}(\bm{\lambda})d\bm{\lambda}\right)$ [STS94, KL01]. In particular, the following Plancherel formula holds. For all $f_{1},f_{2}\in L^{2}\left(\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n},\prod_{i=1}^{n}dx_{i}/x_{i}\right)$ , we have

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}}f_{1}(\bm{x})\overline{f_{2}(\bm{x})}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{{d}x_{i}}{x_{i}}=\int_{(\mathrm{i}\mathbb{R})^{n}}\widehat{f_{1}}(\bm{\lambda})\overline{\widehat{f_{2}}(\bm{\lambda})}s_{n}(\bm{\lambda}){d}\bm{\lambda}. $$

Now we turn to the Whittaker transform of a particular function $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha,\bm{\beta};r}(\bm{x})$ , which naturally appears in the Laplace transform of the point-to-line partition function of trapezoidal polymers, and symmetrized polymers in general, see Remark 2.9.

#### Definition 2.6.

Assume $r>0$ , $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}$ , $\bm{\beta}\in\mathbb{C}^{m}$ . For $\bm{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}$ , consider an array $\bm{z}=(z_{i,j}:1\leqslant i\leqslant m+1,1\leqslant j\leqslant n)$ with fixed bottom row $z_{m+1,j}=x_{j}$ for all $1\leqslant j\leqslant n$ . Define the type of such an array as

$$ \operatorname{type}(\bm{z})_{i}:=\frac{\prod_{j=1}^{n}z_{i+1,j}}{\prod_{j=1}^{n}z_{i,j}}\quad\text{ for }\quad i=1,\ldots,m. $$

Denoting $\operatorname{type}(\bm{z})^{\bm{\beta}}=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\operatorname{type}(\bm{z})_{i}^{\beta_{i}}$ , we define

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\alpha,\bm{\beta};r}(\bm{x}):=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{nm}} \displaystyle\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}(z_{1,i}/r)^{(-1)^{i}}\right)^{\alpha}\operatorname{type}(\bm{z})^{-\bm{\beta}} \displaystyle\times\exp\left(-\frac{r}{z_{1,n}}-\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{z_{i+1,j+1}+z_{i-1,j}}{z_{i,j}}\right)\prod_{i=1}^{m}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{dz_{i,j}}{z_{i,j}}, $$

with the convention that $z_{i,j}=0$ whenever $(i,j)$ is out of the range $1\leqslant i\leqslant m+1,1\leqslant j\leqslant n$ . We also define $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha,\emptyset;r}(\bm{x})=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i}/r)^{(-1)^{i}}\right)^{\alpha}e^{-r/x_{n}}$ .

The well-definedness of $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha,\bm{\beta};r}$ will be shown in Proposition 2.8. See Figure 6 for a visual representation of integral variables $(z_{i,j})$ . The Whittaker transform of $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha,\bm{\beta};r}(\bm{x})$ in the case $\bm{\beta}=\emptyset$ is known and stated in the following proposition.

#### Proposition 2.7 ([Sta01], [OSZ14, Corollary 5.4]).

Suppose $r>0$ , $\bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}$ , $\alpha_{\circ}\in\mathbb{C}$ satisfy $\Re\left(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{\circ}\right)>0$ for all $i$ and $\Re\left(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j}\right)>0$ for all $i>j$ , then

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}(x_{i}/r)^{(-1)^{i}}\right)^{\alpha_{\circ}}e^{-r/x_{n}}\Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{g}\mathfrak{l}_{n}}(\bm{x})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{dx_{i}}{x_{i}}=r^{-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\Gamma\left(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{\circ}\right)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=i+1}^{n}\Gamma\left(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j}\right). $$

*Figure 6. Tableau of integral variables $(z_{i,j})$ with fixed bottom row $z_{m+1,j}=x_{j}$ in the definition of $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha,\bm{\beta};r}(\bm{x})$ , $n=4$ , $m=3$ .*

Now we give the Whittaker transform of $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha,\bm{\beta};r}(\bm{x})$ . The proof for this formula relies on applying gRSK to a symmetric domain not yet introduced, and we postpone the proof to Section 3.2.

#### Proposition 2.8.

Suppose $r>0$ , $\alpha_{\circ}\in\mathbb{C}$ , $\bm{\beta}\in\mathbb{C}^{m}$ , then $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha_{\circ},\bm{\beta};r}(\bm{x})$ is well-defined for almost every $\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0}$ . Furthermore, suppose that $\bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}$ satisfy $\Re{(\alpha_{\circ}+\alpha_{i})}>0$ for all $i\geqslant 1$ , $\Re{(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j})}>0$ for all $1\leqslant i<j\leqslant n$ and $\Re{(\alpha_{i}+\beta_{k})}>0$ for all $1\leqslant i\leqslant n$ , $1\leqslant k\leqslant m$ . We have

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0}}\mathcal{T}_{\alpha_{\circ},\bm{\beta};r}(\bm{x})\Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}}(\bm{x})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{dx_{i}}{x_{i}}=r^{-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\Gamma(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{\circ})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=i+1}^{n}\Gamma(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{k=1}^{m}\Gamma(\alpha_{i}+\beta_{k}). $$

#### Remark 2.9.

Proposition 2.8 shows that the function $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha_{\circ},\bm{\beta};r}(\bm{x})$ is similar to the function $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}^{\tau}(x)$ used in [BBC20] to define the half-space Whittaker process, see Definition 6.7 therein. This is not a surprise, as the proof of Proposition 2.8 in Section 3.2 involves a symmetrized polymer model equivalent to the half-space polymer model considered in [BBC20]. Moreover, one could show by combining Proposition 2.8 and [BBC20, Prop. 6.10] that when $r=1$ , $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha_{\circ},\bm{\beta};r}(\bm{x})$ is exactly the $\tau\to 0$ limit of the function $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha}^{\tau}(x)$ defined in [BBC20], provided that parameters are appropriately matched. Thus, Definition 2.6 provides a Givental’s type integral representation for the function $\mathcal{T}$ involved in the definition of half-space Whittaker processes, while it was defined in [BBC20] only indirectly through its Whittaker transform.

#### 2.3.2. $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}$ -Whittaker functions

We define the $\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}$ -Whittaker functions also by an integral formula due to [GLO07, GLO08]. The integral is over a half-triangular array (Figure 5B) of depth $2n$ ,

$$ \bm{z}=\left(z_{i,j}:1\leqslant i\leqslant 2n,\lfloor i/2\rfloor+1\leqslant j\leqslant i\right). $$

We define the type of such an array as

$$ \operatorname{type}(\bm{z})_{i}:=\frac{\prod_{j=\lfloor i/2\rfloor+1}^{i}z_{i,j}}{\prod_{j=\lfloor(i-1)/2\rfloor+1}^{i-1}z_{i-1,j}}\quad\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,2n. $$

For $\bm{\alpha}=\left(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}\right)\in\mathbb{C}^{n}$ , we denote $\bm{\alpha}^{\pm}:=\left(-\alpha_{1},\alpha_{1},-\alpha_{2},\alpha_{2},\ldots,-\alpha_{n},\alpha_{n}\right)$ and

$$ \operatorname{type}(\bm{z})^{\bm{\alpha}^{\pm}}:=\prod_{i=1}^{2n}\operatorname{type}(\bm{z})_{i}^{{\alpha}^{\pm}_{i}}. $$

Now we define the $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{o}_{2n+1}$ -Whittaker function with parameter $\bm{\alpha}$ via

$$ \Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{so}_{2n+1}}(\bm{x}):=\int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n^{2}}}\operatorname{type}(\bm{z})^{\bm{\alpha}^{\pm}}\exp\left(-\sum_{i=1}^{2n}\sum_{j=\lfloor i/2\rfloor+1}^{i}\frac{z_{i+1,j+1}+z_{i-1,j}}{z_{i,j}}-\sum_{k=1}^{n}z_{2k-1,k}\right)\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leqslant i<2n\\
\lfloor i/2\rfloor<j\leqslant i\end{subarray}}\frac{{d}z_{i,j}}{z_{i,j}}, $$

where on the bottom row $z_{2n,j+\lfloor i/2\rfloor}=x_{j}$ for $1\leqslant j\leqslant\lceil i/2\rceil$ and by convention $z_{i,j}:=0$ whenever $i,j$ is out of the range $1\leqslant i\leqslant 2n,\lfloor i/2\rfloor+1\leqslant j\leqslant i$ . We conclude this subsection with the Whittaker transform of $\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{o}_{2n+1}$ -Whittaker functions.

#### Proposition 2.10 ([BZ19b, Lemma 3.14]).

Suppose $\mu\in\mathbb{C}$ and $\bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{C}^{n}$ are such that $\Re(\mu)>\max_{j}\left|\Re\left(\alpha_{j}\right)\right|$ . Let

$$ g(\bm{x}):=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}\right)^{\mu}\Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{0}_{2n+1}}(\bm{x}), $$

then $g\in L^{2}\left(\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n},\prod_{i=1}^{n}{~d}x_{i}/x_{i}\right)$ and

$$ \widehat{g}(\bm{\lambda}):=\frac{\prod_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n}\Gamma\left(\mu-\lambda_{i}+\alpha_{j}\right)\Gamma\left(\mu-\lambda_{i}-\alpha_{j}\right)}{\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant n}\Gamma\left(2\mu-\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{j}\right)}. $$

#### Remark 2.11.

Several conventions have been used in the literature in order to define Whittaker functions. Our definition for $\Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}}(\bm{x})$ and $\Psi_{\bm{\beta};r}^{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}}(\bm{x})$ are the same as in [OSZ14], but $\Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}}(\bm{x})$ corresponds to $\Psi_{\bm{-\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}}(\bm{x})=\Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}}(\bm{x}^{\prime})$ in [BZ19b] (for $\bm{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n})$ , we use the notation $\bm{x}^{\prime}=(1/x_{n},1/x_{n-1},\dots,1/x_{1})$ ). In [GLO07, GLO08, BC14, BBC20], Whittaker functions are defined in terms of the variables $\log(x_{i})$ and the parameters $\alpha_{\circ},\alpha_{i},\beta_{j}$ are sometimes multiplied by $\pm\mathrm{i}$ .

Our definition of orthogonal Whittaker functions is such that $\Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{0}_{2n+1}}(\bm{x})$ corresponds to $\Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{s}\mathfrak{0}_{2n+1}}(\bm{x}^{\prime})$ in [BZ19b]. In [GLO07, GLO08], orthogonal Whittaker functions are defined in terms of the variables $\log(x_{i})$ .

### 3.2. Whittaker transform of $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha,\bm{\beta};r}$

We prove in this subsection Proposition 2.8, which is required for transforming (3.1) into (3.18). The proof is similar to the proof for Theorem 3.1. But instead of considering a –shape domain, we consider here the –shape index set $\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{I}^{t}$ where

$$ \mathcal{I}:=\{(i,j)\mid 1\leqslant i\leqslant n,i\leqslant j\leqslant n+m\}. $$

Let the weight array $\bm{W}$ be defined on $\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{I}^{t}$ via

$$ W_{i,j}=W_{j,i}\quad\text{and}\quad W_{i,j}^{-1}\sim\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}2\operatorname{Gamma}\left(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{\circ}\right),&1\leqslant i=j\leqslant n,\\
\operatorname{Gamma}\left(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j}\right),&1\leqslant i<j\leqslant n,\\
\operatorname{Gamma}\left(\alpha_{i}+\beta_{j-n}\right),&1\leqslant i\leqslant n,n<j\leqslant n+m.\end{array}\right. $$

We readily see that the joint probability density function of $(W_{i,j})_{i\leqslant j}$ at $(w_{i,j})_{i\leqslant j}$ can be written as $L_{1}\times L_{2}$ , where

$$ \displaystyle L_{1}:= \displaystyle\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(2w_{i,i})^{-\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{\circ}}}{\Gamma(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{\circ})}\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant n}\frac{w_{i,j}^{-\alpha_{i}-\alpha_{j}}}{\Gamma(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j})}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=n+1}^{n+m}\frac{w_{i,j}^{-\alpha_{i}-\beta_{j-n}}}{\Gamma(\alpha_{i}+\beta_{j-n})}, \displaystyle L_{2}:= \displaystyle\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{w_{i,i}}-\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{w_{i,j}}\right)\prod_{i\leqslant j}\frac{1}{w_{i,j}}. $$

In (3.11), we have written $i<j$ under summation symbol instead of $(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}\cap\{i<j\}$ for simplicity of notation. Since $L_{1}L_{2}$ is a probability density,

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n(m+(n+1)/2)}}L_{1}L_{2}\prod_{i,j}dw_{i,j}=1. $$

Observe that, by definition of Gamma functions, (3.12) still holds when the parameters are complex numbers chosen with real parts as in the hypothesis of Proposition 2.8, even though the probabilistic interpretation is lost. In the following we work directly with (3.12).

#### Proof of Proposition 2.8.

Let $\bm{w}$ be a symmetric array defined on $\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{I}^{t}$ with $\mathcal{I}$ being as in (3.9). Let $L_{1},L_{2}$ be as in (3.10), (3.11). We rewrite $L_{1}$ by gathering the $w_{i,j}$ ’s according to their exponent

$$ \displaystyle L_{1}={} \displaystyle C\prod_{i=1}^{n}w_{i,i}^{-\alpha_{\circ}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=i}^{n+m}w_{i,j}^{-\alpha_{i}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=i+1}^{n}w_{i,j}^{-\alpha_{j}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=n+1}^{n+m}w_{i,j}^{-\beta_{j-n}} \displaystyle={} \displaystyle C\prod_{i=1}^{n}w_{i,i}^{-\alpha_{\circ}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=i}^{n+m}w_{i,j}^{-\alpha_{i}}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\prod_{i=j+1}^{n}w_{j,i}^{-\alpha_{i}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\prod_{i=1}^{n}w_{i,j+n}^{-\beta_{j}} \displaystyle={} \displaystyle C\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}w_{i,i}\right)^{-\alpha_{\circ}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n+m}w_{i,j}\right)^{-\alpha_{i}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}w_{i,j+n}\right)^{-\beta_{j}}, $$

where

$$ C=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}2^{\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{\circ}}\Gamma(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{\circ})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=i+1}^{n}\Gamma(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{k=1}^{m}\Gamma(\alpha_{i}+\beta_{k})\right)^{-1}. $$

By symmetry of $\bm{w}$ we have

$$ L_{2}=\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{I}^{t}}\frac{1}{{w_{i,j}}}\right)\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{1}{w_{i,j}}. $$

Now we make a change of variables via gRSK. Let $\bm{T}:=\operatorname{gRSK}(\bm{W})$ and $\bm{t}:=\operatorname{gRSK}(\bm{w})$ . By Proposition 2.5,

$$ \prod_{i=1}^{n}w_{i,i}=4^{-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\prod_{j=1}^{n}t_{j,j}^{(-1)^{n-j}}. $$

By Proposition 2.3 ,

$$ \prod_{j=1}^{n+m}w_{i,j}=\frac{\tau_{n+m-i}}{\tau_{n+m-i+1}}\quad\text{and}\quad\prod_{i=1}^{n}w_{i,j+n}=\frac{\tau_{j}}{\tau_{j-1}}\quad\text{where}\quad\tau_{k}=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}j-i=k\\
(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{I}^{t}\end{subarray}}t_{i,j}. $$

As in (3.5), the sum in $L_{2}$ can be converted to (here the indices $i,j$ are in $\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{I}^{t}$ )

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i,j}w_{i,j}^{-1}=\frac{1}{t_{1,1}}+2\sum_{1<i\leqslant j}\frac{t_{i-1,j}}{t_{i,j}}+2\sum_{i<j}\frac{t_{i,j-1}}{t_{i,j}}. $$

Inserting (3.13), (3.14), (3.15), (3.10), (3.11) into (3.12), and recalling that $(\log w_{i,j})\mapsto(\log t_{i,j})$ is of Jacobian $\pm 1$ (Proposition 2.4), we obtain

$$ \displaystyle 1= \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n(m+(n+1)/2)}}L_{1}L_{2}\prod_{i,j}dw_{i,j} \displaystyle={} \displaystyle C\int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n(m+(n+1)/2)}}\left(4^{-\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\prod_{j=1}^{n}t_{j,j}^{(-1)^{n-j}}\right)^{-\alpha_{\circ}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{\tau_{n+m-i}}{\tau_{n+m-i+1}}\right)^{-\alpha_{i}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\left(\frac{\tau_{j}}{\tau_{j-1}}\right)^{-\beta_{j}} \displaystyle\qquad\times\exp\left(-\frac{1}{2t_{1,1}}-\sum_{1<i\leqslant j}\frac{t_{i-1,j}}{t_{i,j}}-\sum_{i<j}\frac{t_{i,j-1}}{t_{i,j}}\right)\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{dt_{i,j}}{t_{i,j}}. $$

By the change of variables $2t_{i,j}=r^{-1}s_{i,j}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n(m+(n+1)/2)}} \displaystyle\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n}(r/s_{j,j})^{(-1)^{n-j}}\right)^{\alpha_{\circ}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{\tilde{\tau}_{n+m-i}}{\tilde{\tau}_{n+m-i+1}}\right)^{-\alpha_{i}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\left(\frac{\tilde{\tau}_{j}}{\tilde{\tau}_{j-1}}\right)^{-\beta_{j}} \displaystyle\times\exp\left(-\frac{r}{s_{1,1}}-\sum_{1<i\leqslant j}\frac{s_{i-1,j}}{s_{i,j}}-\sum_{i<j}\frac{s_{i,j-1}}{t_{i,j}}\right)\prod_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}}\frac{ds_{i,j}}{s_{i,j}} \displaystyle={} \displaystyle r^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}-\alpha_{i}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\Gamma(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{\circ})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=i+1}^{n}\Gamma(\alpha_{i}+\alpha_{j})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{k=1}^{m}\Gamma(\alpha_{i}+\beta_{k}), $$

where

$$ \tilde{\tau}_{q}:=\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}j-i=q\\
(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{I}^{t}\end{subarray}}s_{i,j}. $$

Applying Fubini’s theorem to (3.16), we obtain that the partial integral

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{nm}}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n}(r/s_{j,j})^{(-1)^{n-j}}\right)^{\alpha_{\circ}} \displaystyle\prod_{j=1}^{m}\left(\frac{\tilde{\tau}_{j}}{\tilde{\tau}_{j-1}}\right)^{-\beta_{j}} \displaystyle\times\exp \displaystyle\left(-\frac{r}{s_{1,1}}-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1<i\leqslant j\\
j\leqslant i+m-1\end{subarray}}\frac{s_{i-1,j}}{s_{i,j}}-\sum_{i<j\leqslant i+m}\frac{s_{i,j-1}}{s_{i,j}}\right)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=i}^{i+m-1}\frac{ds_{i,j}}{s_{i,j}} $$

is convergent for almost every $(s_{i,j})_{\begin{subarray}{c}(i,j)\in\mathcal{I}\\ j\geqslant i+m\end{subarray}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n(n+1)/2}_{>0}$ . By definition of $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha_{\circ},\bm{\beta};r}$ , we recognize that (3.17) is in fact equal to $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha_{\circ},\bm{\beta};r}(s_{n,n+m},\dots,s_{1,1+m})$ (cf. (3.7)). Thus $\mathcal{T}_{\alpha_{\circ},\bm{\beta};r}(\bm{x})$ is well-defined for a.e. $\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0}$ , which concludes the proof of the first claim of Proposition 2.8.

By definition of $\Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}}$ and using the change of variables $s_{i,j}=z_{i-j+m+n,-j+m+n+1}$ , we obtain (cf. (3.8))

$$ \displaystyle\Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}}(s_{n,n+m},\dots,s_{1,1+m})= \displaystyle\quad\int_{\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n((n-1)/2)}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=i+m+1}^{n+m}\frac{ds_{i,j}}{s_{i,j}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{\tilde{\tau}_{n+m-i}}{\tilde{\tau}_{n+m-i+1}}\right)^{-\alpha_{i}}\exp\left(-\sum_{1<i\leqslant j-m}\frac{s_{i-1,j}}{s_{i,j}}-\sum_{i+m<j}\frac{s_{i,j-1}}{s_{i,j}}\right). $$

It thus follows from Fubini’s theorem that the left hand side of (3.16) is equal to

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}_{>0}}\mathcal{T}_{\alpha_{\circ},\bm{\beta};r}(\bm{x})\Psi_{\bm{\alpha}}^{\mathfrak{gl}_{n}}(\bm{x})\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{dx_{i}}{x_{i}}, $$

which, with (3.16), concludes the proof of the second claim of Proposition 2.8. ∎

To prove Theorem 1.4, we compare the Laplace transform of ${Z}^{\raisebox{4.0pt}{\hbox to9.34pt{\vbox to3.65pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 0.4pt\lower-0.4pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}} {}{{}}{} {}{} {}{} {}{} {}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.8pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}\lxSVG@stroke\lxSVG@drawpath@unclipped{M 0 0 L 11.81 0 L 7.87 3.94 L 3.94 3.94 L 0 0}{fill:none} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces \lxSVG@closescope \lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}(n;m)$ , given by Corollary 3.2, to that of the point-to-point partition function $Z(n,n+m+1)$ (as in Definition 1.3), which was computed in [COSZ14]. We will see that the Laplace transforms of the two partition functions are the same, which yields the identity in law when $m\geqslant n-1$ . We then prove the general case by a probabilistic argument.

Consider the weight array

$$ W_{i,j}^{-1}\sim\operatorname{Gamma}({\alpha}_{i}+\widehat{\alpha}_{j})\quad\text{on}\quad\{(i,j)\mid 1\leqslant i\leqslant n,1\leqslant j\leqslant N\} $$

and the point-to-point partition function $Z(n,N)$ defined by this weight array via (1.1). The Laplace transform of $Z(n,N)$ can be expressed as a contour integral.

#### Proposition 4.1 ([COSZ14, Theorem 3.9]).

Suppose $n\leqslant N$ . Suppose ${\alpha}_{1},\dots,{\alpha}_{n}$ , $\widehat{\alpha}_{1},\dots,\widehat{\alpha}_{N}$ are such that ${\alpha}_{i}+\widehat{\alpha}_{j}>0$ for all $i,j$ . Let $Z(n,N)$ be the point-to-point partition function for the log-gamma polymer with weight array (4.1). Let $\mu>\max_{i,j}\{-\widehat{\alpha}_{j},{\alpha}_{i}\}$ . Then for all $r>0$ , the following formula holds

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[e^{-rZ(n,N)}\right]=\int_{(\mu+\mathrm{i}\mathbb{R})^{n}}r^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left({\alpha}_{i}-\lambda_{i}\right)}\prod_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n}\Gamma\left(\lambda_{i}-{\alpha}_{j}\right)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\Gamma\left(\lambda_{i}+\widehat{\alpha}_{j}\right)}{\Gamma\left({\alpha}_{i}+\widehat{\alpha}_{j}\right)}s_{n}(\bm{\lambda})d\bm{\lambda}. $$

#### Proof.

In [COSZ14], it is proved that if ${\alpha}_{1},\dots,{\alpha}_{n}<0$ and $\widehat{\alpha}_{1},\dots,\widehat{\alpha}_{N}>0$ , then

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[e^{-rZ(n,N)}\right]=\int_{(\mathrm{i}\mathbb{R})^{n}}r^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left({\alpha}_{i}-\lambda_{i}\right)}\prod_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n}\Gamma\left(\lambda_{i}-{\alpha}_{j}\right)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\Gamma\left(\lambda_{i}+\widehat{\alpha}_{j}\right)}{\Gamma\left({\alpha}_{i}+\widehat{\alpha}_{j}\right)}s_{n}(\bm{\lambda})d\bm{\lambda}. $$

In the general case, note that ${\alpha}_{i}+\widehat{\alpha}_{j}=({\alpha}_{i}-\mu)+(\widehat{\alpha}_{j}+\mu)$ . We may therefore apply the preceding formula to $({\alpha}_{i}-\mu)_{i}$ and $(\widehat{\alpha}_{j}+\mu)_{j}$

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[e^{-rZ(n,N)}\right]=\int_{(\mathrm{i}\mathbb{R})^{n}}r^{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left({\alpha}_{i}-\mu-\lambda_{i}\right)}\prod_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n}\Gamma\left(\lambda_{i}+\mu-{\alpha}_{j}\right)\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{j=1}^{N}\frac{\Gamma\left(\lambda_{i}+\widehat{\alpha}_{j}+\mu\right)}{\Gamma\left({\alpha}_{i}+\widehat{\alpha}_{j}\right)}s_{n}(\bm{\lambda})d\bm{\lambda}. $$

The change of variable $\bm{\lambda}\mapsto\bm{\lambda}-\mu$ then completes the proof. ∎

Step 1.
